text: They were rushing to give a talk about kindness.
Some stepped right over a man who needed help.
In 1973, Princeton psychologists John Darley and Daniel Batson published the study.
Their subjects: seminary students.
Each had to walk to another building and give a short talk.
For some, the topic was the Good Samaritan. Stopping for a stranger.
Then the switch. Some were told they had time. Others: you're late. Hurry.
In an alley on the way, a man sat slumped in a doorway. He coughed. He groaned.
With time to spare, sixty-three percent stopped to help.
In a hurry? Ten percent.
The Good Samaritan talk? No significant difference.
In this study, the clock mattered more than the sermon.
Later, almost all of them remembered him.
They saw him. Their minds just never caught up.
The researchers compared it to a narrowing map.
You do this every day.
The text you'll answer later. The face you didn't look at. The question you rushed past.
But it isn't who you are. It's how fast you're moving.
One small study. Forty students. But you've felt it.
Tomorrow, leave five minutes early.
Spend them looking up.
So who did you walk past today?
